To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
epileptiform activity in children with continuous spike-wave during slow sleep is associated with a widespread activation and deactivation of brain networks.
children with continuous spikes during sleep demonstrate a highly significant activation of the perislyvan brain regions and deactivation of the structures of the default-mode network.

the neuronal networks in children with symptomatic or cryptogenic continuous spikes during slow sleep are characterized by activation of both perisylvian and cingulate cortex, as well as by deactivation of structures of the default-mode network.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new approach for studying the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying epileptic encephalopathies with continuous epileptiform activity.
the functional neuroanatomy of the epileptic activity in children with continuous spike and waves during slow-wave sleep.
the functional organization of neuronal networks in children with symptomatic or cryptogenic continuous spikes during slow sleep.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

epileptic activity during slow sleep is not only associated with the activation of neuronal network but also with the deactivation of neuronal network, and this deactivation may contribute to neuropsychological deficits.
continuous spikes and waves in slow sleep are associated with the activation of the perisylvalian network, and the deactivation of the default mode and fronto-parietal networks.
the epileptiform discharging network is characterized by the involvement of the perisyvian brain regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
continuous spikes and waves are not a simple epileptiform discharge.

continuous spikes and waves in slow sleep is associated with activation of a neuronal network that involves both the epileptic focus and the surrounding areas, and deactivation of the default mode networks.

the continuous spikes and waves in sleep are associated with a highly significant activation of a neuronal network involving the perisylvan region, insula, cingulate gyrush and deactivation of structures of default mode network.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the functional magnetic resonance imaging findings in children with continuous spike and waves during slow wave sleep are similar to those observed in other types of epileptic disorders.
the haemodynamic response to epileptic discharges in children with continuous spike and waves during slow wave sleep is similar to the haemodynamic correlates of the epileptic activity in adults.

the epileptic discharges are associated with a highly significant and reproducible haemodynamic response, which is similar in children with different aetiologies of continuous spikes and slow-wave sleep.
